To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transgenic growth‐deficient (Tgr) rat, a dwarf strain that has a reduced number of GH‐releasing factor (GHRH)-producing neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC), shows increased hypothalamic tubero‐infundibular dopaminergie (TIDA) neurons, despite reduced pituitary Prolatein (PRL) content.

(i) in the Tgr rat, a model in which the hGH transgenic is targeted to GHRH neurons, the lactogenic feedback effect is increased and this is reflected in increased TH and DA in the TIDA neurones; and (ii) in the dw/dw rat, a model with a pituitary GH deficiency, the lactogenic effect is reduced and this is reflected by a decreased number of TH‐immunoactive TIDA neurone.
the Tgr dwarf rats have a reduced number of GHRH neurone and increased number of TIDA neurons in their median eminence, and that the Tgr rats have reduced PRL levels in the pituitary gland.

the role of the hypothalamus in the regulation of growth hormone (GH) secretion.
understanding how the hypothalamic regulation of pituitary prolac- tin (PRL) secretion is altered in two rat models of dwarfism, the TGR rat (transgenic growth retarded) and dw/dw rat (dwarka dwarf).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TIDA neurones are not affected in the dw/dw rats and that the TIDA system is activated in the Tgr rats, which is in agreement with the lactogenic feedback hypothesis.
the changes in TIDA cells in these two dwarf models of dwarfism is due to the combined effect of the primary changes in the somatotropic system (GHRH and GH) and lactotropic system (PRL).
the lactogenic feedback effect is mediated by the hypothalamic GHRH neurone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lactogenic feedback in the TGR model is more effective than that in the dw/dw model.
lactogenic feedback in the rat is mediated by the hypothalamic TIDAs, whereas somatogenic feedback is mediated by the GHRH neurone.
the lactogenic effect of GH on TIDA neurones is not a consequence of the dwarfism per se, but rather reflects the lactogenic action of GH on the lactotrophs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TGR model is not a good model for studying the regulation of the lactotropes.
we can now use the Tgr rat model to understand the effects of GH deficiency and hypersecretion on the pituitary gland.
the hypothalamic Tida neurons, which regulate prolactin release, can be stimulated by growth hormone.
